title: Burst cost + latency scenario catalogue (informal)
content:
Purpose
This is a working catalogue of microburst / short-lived spike scenarios and the latency vs cost tradeoffs we observed across three serving configurations. The goal is to produce short collateral we can reuse in internal runbooks and in the Optimize product docs (drafts). Not a formal report — think of this as a bench-notes + sketch for outreach and product copy.

Scope and quick summary
- Workload: chat-style requests (turns) with heavy tail on long context reuse. 75% short-turn (<=40 tokens), 20% medium (40-250 tokens), 5% long (>=250 tokens).
- Concurrency patterns: microbursts (50–500 qps for 5–30s), steady baseline (10–40 qps), sessionized bursts (concurrency spikes per-session).
- Models: baseline FP16 large-open model, quantized-int8 variant, and a distilled small model for fallback.
- Platforms evaluated: Core cluster (dense GPUs), Edge pool (near-user nodes), and Dedicated reserve pool (pre-warmed).

Key observations (high level)
1) Microburst latency tails are dominated by queueing during the first 1–3 seconds of spike; warm-starts reduce p50 but only modestly affect p99 without capacity.
2) Quantization (int8) reduces per-token energy/cost by ~22–32% depending on sequence length, but increases p99 by 8–18 ms in Core and by ~15–35 ms in Edge nodes (smaller VRAM/CPU contention).
3) Dedicated pre-warmed pools drastically reduce p99 for sub-second bursts — p99 improvement is ~35–60% vs. on-demand Core, at a monthly capacity reservation cost.
4) Fallback to the distilled model keeps latency within SLO for most short-turn bursts, but quality regressions appear for medium/long context turns (qual diffs noted in evals).

Methodology notes (quick)
- Synthetic traffic generated by bench-scripts v0.9 (docs in linked PR). Mix uses poisson arrival with injected deterministic spike window.
- Each scenario ran 4x for 10 minutes, with a 15-minute cool-down between runs to clear caches. We recorded per-request timestamps, queuing time, compute time, and token counts.
- Cost model: marginal GPU-time + amortized pre-warm cost (for Dedicated) + small network overhead. Reported as USD per 1k tokens and USD per 10k short-turn queries.

ASCII charts (text representation)
1) p50/p90/p99 during a 30s microburst (50->400qps ramp) — normalized to steady baseline (1.0):

   Config      p50    p90    p99
   ---------  ----   ----   ----
   Core-FP16   1.1    1.6    2.4
   Core-INT8   1.0    1.7    2.6
   Edge-FP16   1.3    2.1    3.2
   Edge-INT8   1.2    2.4    3.7
   Dedicated   1.0    1.1    1.4

Interpretation: Dedicated keeps tails close to baseline; Edge shows highest p99 amplification during short spikes, and quantization slightly worsens tails on smaller nodes.

2) Cost per 1k tokens vs p99 (scatter-ish table):

   Config        $/1k tok   p99 (ms)
   ------------  ---------  -------
   Core-FP16       0.95      520
   Core-INT8       0.72      540
   Edge-FP16       1.12      710
   Edge-INT8       0.83      740
   Dedicated       1.48      210  (includes reservation amort)
   Distilled       0.34      180

Notes: Dedicated is more expensive per-token when amortized, but provides the tightest latency envelope. Distilled model is cheap & low-latency but has meaningful quality delta (see "quality notes").

Quality notes (very informal)
- We ran 200 eval prompts for medium/long context; distilled model has 18% higher hallucination rate on our metrics vs Core-FP16. For purely short-turn UIs (<=40 tokens) quality differences are negligible.
- Recommendation: use distilled fallback only as last resort for strict-latency SLOs or to handle overflow; flag requests for review where fallback activated >5% of session requests.

Scenario catalogue (short forms)
- Scenario A: Sudden city-wide event (news spike) — long tail on medium messages. Characteristics: 300–500 qps for 20–40s; mixture leans heavier to medium. Impact: Edge p99 x3, Core p99 x2.4. Mitigation: route to Dedicated pools or enable auto-burst to Core reserve.
- Scenario B: Product launch funnel (sessionized) — many new sessions, low-turn length. Characteristics: many short turns, concurrency per user low, aggregate spiky QPS. Impact: queueing dominates; distilled fallback effective. Mitigation: small-batch windowing and aggressive prefetch-caching of common prompts.
- Scenario C: Background batch generation (sustained) — not a microburst but sustained high-concurrency. Characteristics: 1–3k qps sustained over hours. Impact: cost scale dominates; use quantized and spot burst autoscaling.

Playbook snippets (for SRE / solutions)
- If p99>SLO during microburst: 1) check queue length and pre-warm signals, 2) temporarily increase fast-fallback to distilled for short-turn routes, 3) failover sessions to Dedicated if configured, 4) post-mortem: root-cause whether we hit slot-count limits or kernel contention.
- SLO policy suggestion: allow 15% ephemeral p99 degradation for <=30s microbursts if fallbacks are enabled; otherwise route to higher-tier capacity.

Open questions / TODO (what I want to follow up)
- Produce a small synthetic artifact showing per-token energy delta (FP16 vs INT8) across sequence length sweep — we have partial logs but not normalized. (todo: Samir to run sweep w/ per-kernel counters)
- Need clearer amortization math for Dedicated — current estimate uses 70% utilization; but many customers see <40% sustained. Should show both 40% and 70% scenarios.
- Add real-user session traces (anonymized) to validate synthetic mixes. Buyer-concern: does our synthetic burst reflect real burst shapes?
- Nail down recommended default fallback thresholds (p99 delta % to trigger distilled) and expose in Console.

Audience-ready bullets (1-paragraph summaries for product copy)
- If you need predictable tails during short spikes, Dedicated pre-warmed pools are the fastest way to reduce extreme latency at the cost of reserved capacity. For teams who prefer usage-only costs, Core with quantization reduces per-token spend but expects wider tails during microbursts and may need software fallbacks. For UI flows dominated by short-turns, a small distilled fallback can preserve user-perceived latency cheaply, but beware quality regressions on longer context turns.
- Avoid using the word "best" without qualifiers; use "lowest-tail" or "lowest-latency-envelope" since cost+quality space is multi-dimensional.

Appendix: quick wiring diagrams (text)
- Route policy example:
   client -> edge-lb -> fast-path: (dedicated if available) -> core-fallback -> distilled-fallback -> reject/queue

- Basic metric set to collect for each route:
   - qps, concurrent slots, avg queue time, kernel-sched-wait, token/s, p50/p90/p99, fallback-rate, cost_per_1k_tokens

Rough notes to self
- This doc should feed into: 1) the Optimize micro-article on fallbacks, 2) the internal SRE runbook (short form), 3) a short slide for sales to talk through cost/latency tradeoffs per-customer case.
- Avoid using the word "best" without qualifiers; use "lowest-tail" or "lowest-latency-envelope" since cost+quality space is multi-dimensional.

End of catalogue draft — feedback welcome.
